481: void IndexRecJPQPrune::reset() {
482:     item_codes.clear();
483:     ids.clear();
484:     invlists.clear();
485:     ntotal = 0;
486:     ids_sequential = true;
487:     {
488:         std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(id_map_mutex);
489:         id_to_pos.clear();
490:         id_map_built = false;
491:     }
492:     // the codebooks are kept: they are part of the index configuration
493: }
494: 
495: idx_t IndexRecJPQPrune::position_of_id(idx_t key) const {
496:     if (ids_sequential) {
497:         FAISS_THROW_IF_NOT_FMT(
498:                 key >= 0 && key < ntotal,
499:                 "unknown id %" PRId64,
500:                 key);
501:         return key;
502:     }
503:     std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(id_map_mutex);
504:     if (!id_map_built) {
505:         id_to_pos.reserve(ids.size());
506:         for (size_t i = 0; i < ids.size(); i++) {
507:             id_to_pos[ids[i]] = (idx_t)i;
508:         }
509:         id_map_built = true;
510:     }
511:     auto it = id_to_pos.find(key);
512:     FAISS_THROW_IF_NOT_FMT(
513:             it != id_to_pos.end(), "unknown id %" PRId64, key);
514:     return it->second;
515: }

517: void IndexRecJPQPrune::reconstruct_positions(
518:         idx_t i0,
519:         idx_t ni,
520:         float* recons) const {
521:     FAISS_THROW_IF_NOT_MSG(
522:             i0 >= 0 && i0 + ni <= ntotal,
523:             "IndexRecJPQPrune::reconstruct_positions: range out of bounds");
524:     for (idx_t i = 0; i < ni; i++) {
525:         float* r = recons + (size_t)i * d;
526:         const uint8_t* c = item_codes.data() + ((size_t)i0 + i) * M;
527:         for (size_t m = 0; m < M; m++) {
528:             std::memcpy(
529:                     r + m * d_split,
530:                     codebooks.data() + ((size_t)m * B + c[m]) * d_split,
531:                     d_split * sizeof(float));
532:         }
533:     }
534: }
535: 
536: void IndexRecJPQPrune::reconstruct(idx_t key, float* recons) const {
537:     const idx_t pos = position_of_id(key);
538:     reconstruct_positions(pos, 1, recons);
539: }
540: 
541: void IndexRecJPQPrune::reconstruct_n(idx_t i0, idx_t ni, float* recons) const {
542:     // Faiss convention: i0 .. i0 + ni - 1 are external ids
543:     std::vector<idx_t> pos(ni);
544:     for (idx_t i = 0; i < ni; i++) {
545:         pos[i] = position_of_id(i0 + i);
546:     }
547:     for (idx_t i = 0; i < ni; i++) {
548:         reconstruct_positions(pos[i], 1, recons + (size_t)i * d);
549:     }
550: }
551: 
552: void IndexRecJPQPrune::reconstruct_batch(
553:         idx_t n,
554:         const idx_t* keys,
555:         float* recons) const {
556:     for (idx_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
557:         reconstruct(keys[i], recons + (size_t)i * d);
558:     }
559: }
560: 
561: size_t IndexRecJPQPrune::memory_footprint() const {
562:     return item_codes.size() * sizeof(uint8_t) +
563:             ids.size() * sizeof(idx_t) + codebooks.size() * sizeof(float) +
564:             invlists.offsets.size() * sizeof(size_t) +
565:             invlists.item_ids.size() * sizeof(idx_t);
566: }

Hmm, that's a real problem: a B×1 column-major matrix with ldc=1 is invalid per the BLAS standard ("for a column-major m×n matrix, ldc >= max(1,m)"). The standard says leading dimension >= max(1, m). So we can't legally pass ldc=1 when m=B>1.

Solution:

  1. Swap the roles: compute C as n×m instead… i.e., compute a B×1 column vector. Alternative formulation: compute row b of S_m… Let me think of the math again.

S_m (B vectors of dim d_split) = G_m * x_m, where G_m is B×d_split row-major.

Option A: call sgemm per split with m=B, n=1, k=d_split, C = S_m (B×1). Need ldc >= B. S_m's memory is B contiguous floats, so with ldc=B it would write to C[i,0] = C + i*B — wrong, it would stride by B!

Wait, no. C[i,0] is at offset ildc = iB. But S_m's element b is at offset b (contiguous). So with ldc=B we'd be writing the b-th element at offset b*B — wrong.

Hmm, I see — so a B×1 result cannot be written contiguously with a legal ldc… except when we consider that in the actual layout the C matrix is 1×B (row-major B) = column-major 1×B, i.e., m'=1, n'=B. Let me reformulate:

Compute C' (1×B column-major) = A' * B' with:

  • A' (1×d_split) = x_m^T… hmm: C'[0,b] = sum_j x_m[j] * G_m[b,j].
  • C' = A' (1×d_split) × B' (d_split×B), where B'[j,b] = G_m[b,j].
  • G_m row-major (B×d_split) = G_m column-major (d_split×B). So B' = the G_m block itself, ldb = d_split.
  • A' = x_m as 1×d_split, lda = d_split (or 1).
  • So: sgemm_("N","N", m=1, n=B, k=d_split, alpha, x_m, lda=d_split, G_m, ldb=d_split, beta, S_m, ldc=B).

This is legal: C is 1×B, ldc >= max(1, m=1) → ldc=B is fine. And C[0,b] is at offset b → S_m is written contiguously.

So the call is: m=1, n=B, k=d_split, no transposes:

sgemm_("Not transposed", "Not transposed",
        &m1, &nB, &kds,
        &one,
        x + m*d_split,        // A: 1 x d_split, lda = d_split
        &lda,
        codebooks + m*B*d_split, // B: d_split x B (cm view of row-major B x d_split), ldb = d_split
        &ldb,
        &zero,
        S + m*B,              // C: 1 x B, ldc = B
        &ldc_B);

where m1=1, nB=B, kds=d_split, lda=d_split, ldb=d_split, ldc=B.

Verify: C[0,b] = sum_j A[0,j] B[j,b] = sum_j x_m[j] G_m_cm[j,b] = sum_j x_m[j] * G_m_rm[b,j] = dot(x_m, G_m[b]). ✓

Or even simpler, Option B: just loop over b and use sdot per sub-item: S_m[b] = dot(x_m, G_m[b]) via sgemm with n=B… that's exactly what Option A is. OK, going with Option A.

Actually wait, even simpler and most robust: use cblas_sdot? No, that still needs cblas.h. sgemm with m=1, n=B, k=d_split is the clean BLAS way (that's exactly what "a row vector times a matrix" is).

19: /** CSR (compressed sparse row) inverted lists for IndexRecJPQPrune.
20:  *
21:  * The catalogue of N items is represented by a row-major N x M matrix of
22:  * item codes; the code at split m of item i is in [0, B).  There are
23:  * M * B posting lists, identified by
24:  *
25:  *     list_id = split * B + sub_item_id
26:  *
27:  * The posting list of (split, sub_item_id) contains the internal positions
28:  * of all items whose code at that split equals sub_item_id.
29:  *
30:  * Storage is CSR-style:
31:  *
32:  *     offsets has M * B + 1 entries;
33:  *     the items of list l are item_ids[offsets[l] .. offsets[l + 1]).
34:  *
35:  * The storage is dense and unpadded: no slot is reserved for empty posting
36:  * lists and there is at most one heap allocation for all list contents (and
37:  * one for the offsets). Within each posting list, item positions appear in
38:  * ascending order (the order in which items were added), which makes the
39:  * lists amenable to sequential access.
40:  */
41: struct RecJPQInvertedLists {
42:     size_t M = 0; ///< number of splits
43:     size_t B = 0; ///< number of sub-item ids per split
44: 
45:     /** offsets of the M * B + 1 posting list boundaries */
46:     std::vector<size_t> offsets;
47:     /** concatenation of all posting lists: N * M entries after build */
48:     std::vector<idx_t> item_ids;
49: 
50:     /** Two-pass construction from a row-major N x M uint8 code matrix.
51:      *
52:      * The first pass counts the items per posting list, a prefix sum turns
53:      * the counts into offsets and the second pass fills the contiguous
54:      * item storage. Item positions are preserved in ascending order.
55:      *
56:      * @param item_codes  N * M codes, the code at split m of item i is at
57:      *                    item_codes[i * M + m], must be in [0, B)
58:      * @param N           number of items
59:      * @param M           number of splits, >= 1
60:      * @param B           number of sub-item ids per split, in [1, 256]
61:      */
62:     void build(const uint8_t* item_codes, size_t N, size_t M, size_t B);
63: 
64:     /** Drop all postings and metadata. */
65:     void clear();
66: 
67:     /// number of items in the posting list (split, sub_item_id)
68:     size_t list_size(size_t split, size_t sub_item_id) const;
69: 
70:     /// pointer to the first entry of the posting list (nullptr when the
71:     /// list is empty or the lists have not been built)
72:     const idx_t* get_list(size_t split, size_t sub_item_id) const;
73: 
74:     /// half-open range [begin, end) of the posting list contents
75:     std::pair<const idx_t*, const idx_t*> get_list_range(
76:             size_t split,
77:             size_t sub_item_id) const;
78: 
79:     /// total number of postings (= N * M after a build)
80:     size_t total_entries() const {
81:         return item_ids.size();
82:     }
83: };

const idx_t* RecJPQInvertedLists::get_list(
        size_t split,

    FAISS_THROW_IF_NOT(split < M);

The base class documentation for reconstruct_n says "Reconstructs vectors from i0 to i0 + ni - 1" and "@param i0 index of the first vector in the sequence". "Index of the first vector in the sequence" — this is position-based (a contiguous range of stored vectors), not an arbitrary external ID. The base implementation:

void Index::reconstruct_n(idx_t i0, idx_t ni, float* recons) const {
    for (idx_t i = 0; i < ni; i++) {
        reconstruct(i0 + i, recons + i * d);
    }
}

Hmm — the base implementation calls reconstruct(i0 + i) using ID semantics. That is, the base implementation treats i0+i as an ID (key). This is faiss's (somewhat confusing) convention: the base reconstruct_n interprets the range as consecutive external IDs.

Let me check IndexIDMapTemplate — does it override reconstruct_n? From the grep results, only reconstruct is overridden (line 420). So IndexIDMap does not override reconstruct_n, and the base implementation calls this->reconstruct(i0+i) → IndexIDMap::reconstruct(i0+i) → ID semantics. In other words, in IndexIDMap (a canonical index with external IDs), reconstruct_n(i0, ni) reconstructs items with external IDs i0..i0+ni-1.

Therefore, my implementation (treating i0..i0+ni-1 as external IDs via position_of_id) matches the effective behavior of the base class in an index with IDs. Good — this is consistent with the earlier decision recorded in the summary ("reconstruct_n ... (Faiss convention for external IDs)").

function(link_to_faiss_lib target)
  if(NOT FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "avx2" AND NOT FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "avx512" AND NOT FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "avx512_spr" AND NOT FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "sve" AND NOT FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "dd")
    target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE faiss)
  endif()

  if(FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "avx2")
    if(NOT WIN32)
      target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:-mavx2 -mfma>)
    else()
      target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:/arch:AVX2>)
    endif()
    target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE faiss_avx2)
  endif()

  if(FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "avx512")
    if(NOT WIN32)
      target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:-mavx2 -mfma -mavx512f -mavx512f -mavx512cd -mavx512vl -mavx512dq -mavx512bw>)
    else()
      target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:/arch:AVX512>)
    endif()
    target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE faiss_avx512)
  endif()

  if(FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "avx512_spr")
    if(NOT WIN32)
      # Architecture mode to support AVX512 extensions available since Intel (R) Sapphire Rapids.
      # Ref: https://networkbuilders.intel.com/solutionslibrary/intel-avx-512-fp16-instruction-set-for-intel-xeon-processor-based-products-technology-guide
      target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:-mavx2 -mfma -mf16c -mavx512f -mavx512cd -mavx512vl -mavx512dq -mavx512bw -mavx512vpopcntdq -mavx512bitalg -mpopcnt -mavx512fp16 -mavx512bf16>)
    else()
      target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:/arch:AVX512>)
    endif()
    target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE faiss_avx512_spr)
  endif()

  if(FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "sve")
    if(NOT WIN32)
      if("${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} ${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG} " MATCHES "(^| )-march=native")
        # Do nothing, expect SVE to be enabled by -march=native
      elseif("${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} ${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG} " MATCHES "(^| )(-march=armv[0-9]+(\\.[1-9]+)?-[^+ ](\\+[^+$ ]+)*)")
        # Add +sve
        target_compile_options(${target}  PRIVATE $<$<AND:$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>,$<CONFIG:DEBUG>>:${CMAKE_MATCH_2}+sve>)
      elseif(NOT "${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} ${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG} " MATCHES "(^| )-march=armv")
        # No valid -march, so specify -march=armv8-a+sve as the default
        target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<AND:$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>,$<CONFIG:DEBUG>>:-march=armv8-a+sve>)
      endif()
      if("${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} ${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE} " MATCHES "(^| )-march=native")
        # Do nothing, expect SVE to be enabled by -march=native
      elseif("${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} ${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE} " MATCHES "(^| )(-march=armv[0-9]+(\\.[1-9]+)?-[^+ ](\\+[^+$ ]+)*)")
        # Add +sve
        target_compile_options(${target}  PRIVATE $<$<AND:$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>,$<CONFIG:RELEASE>>:${CMAKE_MATCH_2}+sve>)
      elseif(NOT "${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS} ${CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE} " MATCHES "(^| )-march=armv")
        # No valid -march, so specify -march=armv8-a+sve as the default
        target_compile_options(${target} PRIVATE $<$<AND:$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>,$<CONFIG:RELEASE>>:-march=armv8-a+sve>)
      endif()
    else()
      # TODO: support Windows
    endif()
    target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE faiss_sve)
  endif()

  if(FAISS_OPT_LEVEL STREQUAL "dd")
    # DD mode: link to main faiss library with DD-specific definitions
    # When FAISS_OPT_LEVEL=dd, the main faiss library is built with DD enabled,
    # so we link to faiss (not a separate faiss_dd).
    # FAISS_ENABLE_DD exposes SIMDConfig class to consuming code (e.g., tests)
    # COMPILE_SIMD_* flags enable DD code paths in headers (architecture-specific)
    # Note: No SIMD compile flags here - DD handles dispatch internally.
    # Special tests (like test_simd_levels.cpp) that use raw intrinsics
    # should get their own SIMD flags via set_source_files_properties.
    #
    # Architecture-specific definitions mirror simd_dispatch.bzl dispatch_config:
    # - x86_64: AVX2 + AVX512 enabled
    # - aarch64: ARM_NEON enabled
    target_compile_definitions(${target} PRIVATE FAISS_ENABLE_DD)
    if(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR MATCHES "(x86_64|amd64|AMD64)")
      target_compile_definitions(${target} PRIVATE COMPILE_SIMD_AVX2 COMPILE_SIMD_AVX512)
    elseif(CMAKE_SYSTEM_PROCESSOR MATCHES "(aarch64|arm64|ARM64)")
      target_compile_definitions(${target} PRIVATE COMPILE_SIMD_ARM_NEON)
    endif()
    target_link_libraries(${target} PRIVATE faiss)
  endif()
endfunction()

Wait — the exhaustive baseline: score all N items with S lookup: N*M additions. For N=1M, M=8, that's 8M lookups per query — no problem.

For the "exact match check", compare RecJPQPrune's top-k with the exhaustive baseline's top-k: compare the multiset of scores (rank-sorted) with a tolerance, and compare the set of ids when there's no tie at the boundary. Simpler: compare the sorted list of top-k scores with a relative error tolerance of ~1e-5, and additionally verify that the sum of top-k scores matches. Actually, the simplest and most robust check: the score at rank k-1 (the threshold) from both, and the number of items with score greater than the threshold must be equal. Let's do it this way: compute exhaustive top-k scores (descending), and RecJPQ top-k scores (descending), and check max |diff| < 1e-4 (float tolerance) — that's a strong signal of exact match.

For the baseline timing, I want "exhaustive PQTopK" = score all N items + topk selection (partial_sort of N entries). That's the honest baseline the paper compares against.

Per-BS stats: for each BS in {1,2,4,8,16,32,64}:

  • Run nq queries, each via a separate search() call with k=k (to measure per-query latency).
  • Collect per-query latencies → median, p95.
  • Aggregate stats: total iterations, total scored items, total traversed postings, sub-items processed; report the average per query and the catalog ratio = avg items_scored / N.

To keep runtimes reasonable: N=1M, nq=100, 7 BS values → 700 searches. Each search in the worst case (BS=1) could score a large fraction of the catalog... hmm, in random data with k=100 out of N=1M, how much does pruning work? The paper shows dramatic reductions on real recommendation data; on random data the reduction is modest. BS=1 might score a lot of items. Let me estimate: each iteration processes BS sub-items from one split, and each sub-item's posting list has N/B = ~3900 items. After ~k/B-ish... hard to estimate; in the worst case we end up scoring a large fraction. 100 queries × (up to ~N×M lookups) = could be slow, but in a release build scoring is fast (simple additions): 1M items × 8 lookups = 8M adds ≈ a few ms. Even if we score 50% of the catalog per query: 4M adds ≈ ~2ms. 700 queries ≈ a few seconds. No problem.

Also, measure build time (CSR construction) and report memory_footprint.

Also, as a sanity check, include the time of an "IndexFlatCodes" style baseline? Nah — keep it to the PQTopK exhaustive baseline that the paper uses.

Also, to follow the style note in bench_rabitq_batch_estimates.cpp ("run with OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1"), note in the header comment that BLAS is only used for S computation (M small sgemvs) — OpenBLAS threading could add noise; recommend single-thread.

So, let's write the bench. Use std::chrono, percentile computation, and plain printf output.

One important detail: search() is called per query — each call is one query (n=1). The stats accumulate per call; reset stats per query and collect.

Also add a correctness check at the end: for the first ~8 queries, compare the top-k score vector against the exhaustive baseline.

For the baseline: compute S per query using idx.compute_sub_item_scores, then score all N items with a score_item loop — but score_item is per-item (a method that checks bounds). In the benchmark, do it inline for speed:

std::vector<float> scores(N);

for (idx_t i = 0; i < N; i++) {

    scores[i] = s;
}
// top-k via partial_sort of indices

partial_sort of 1M entries per query — 100 queries — no problem (~ms each).

Actually, to keep the bench simple and robust, use std::nth_element + partial_sort of the top k by score (with position as tiebreaker). For the comparison with RecJPQPrune's output, compare only the sorted score values (with tolerance) — ties in id ordering are policy-dependent, so comparing scores is the exact-match invariant. Plus, when the k-th boundary is strict, compare the id sets too. To keep the code simple: compare top-k score vectors with tolerance, plus check that the number of items with score above the threshold matches (which is the case if the score vectors match).

Codes are uniform, codebooks and queries are unit-norm\n// Gaussian; random data is a hard case for the pruning (no\n// cluster structure), so the pruning ratios here are conservative.\n//\n// For stable timings run with a single BLAS/OpenMP thread:\n//   OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 ./bench_recjpq_prune\n\n#include <algorithm>\n#include <chrono>\n#include <cmath>\n#include <cstdio>\n#include <cstring>\n#include <random>\n#include <vector>\n\n#include <faiss/IndexRecJPQPrune.h>\n\nnamespace {\n\nusing Clock = std::chrono::steady_clock;\n\ndouble ms_since(Clock::time_point t0) {\n    return std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(Clock::now() - t0).count();\n}\n\nfloat percentile(std::vector<double>& v, double p) {\n    std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());\n    if (v.empty()) {\n        return 0.0;\n    }\n    const size_t idx =\n            std::min<size_t>(v.size() - 1, (size_t)std::llround(p / 100.0 *\n                                                                  (v.size() - 1)));\n    return (float)v[idx];\n}\n\n/// exhaustive PQTopK: score every item with the S lookup table and\n/// return the k best (score, position) pairs in descending score order\nstruct ExhaustiveTopK {\n    std::vector<float> scores; ///< k, descending\n    std::vector<int64_t> positions; ///< k\n};\n\nExhaustiveTopK exhaustive_search(\n        const faiss::IndexRecJPQPrune& idx,\n        const std::vector<float>& S,\n        int64_t k) {\n    const int64_t N = idx.ntotal;\n    const size_t M = idx.M;\n    const size_t B = idx.B;\n    const uint8_t* codes = idx.item_codes.data();\n\n    std::vector<float> all_scores((size_t)N);\n    for (int64_t i = 0; {
  "content": "# IndexRecJPQPrune: exact top-K search over RecJPQ embeddings with dynamic pruning\n\nFaiss implementation of the dynamic pruning search algorithm from\n**\"Efficient Recommendation with Millions of Items by Dynamic Pruning of\nSub-Item Embeddings\"** (Petrov, Macdonald, Tonellotto, SIGIR 2025,\n[arXiv:2505.00560](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00560)), for catalogues of\nitems whose embeddings are compressed with RecJPQ (Rec-Joint Product\nQuantization).\n\n- Class: `faiss::IndexRecJPQPrune` in `faiss/IndexRecJPQPrune.h`\n- Inverted lists: `faiss::RecJPQInvertedLists` in `faiss/invlists/RecJPQInvertedLists.h`\n- Tests: `tests/test_recjpq_prune.cpp` (22 tests)\n- Benchmark: `benchs/bench_recjpq_prune.cpp`\n- Demo: `demos/demo_recjpq_prune.cpp`\n\n## Data model\n\nEach of the `N` items is represented by `M` codes (one per *split*), each a\n`uint8_t` in `[0, B)` (hence `B <= 256`). The (approximate) embedding of an\nitem is the concatenation of its `M` *sub-item embeddings* looked up from the\ncodebooks:\n\n```\nembedding(i) = concat( G[0][code(i,0)], G[1][code(i,1)], ..., G[M-1][code(i,M-1)] )\n```\n\nwith `G[m]` an `B x d_split` codebook and `d_split = d / M`. Only\n`METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT` is supported (higher score is better); results are\nreturned in descending score order, padded with `(-1, -inf)` when fewer than\n`k` items exist.\n\nThe index is *built from pre-computed codes and codebooks* (typically from an\nexisting `IndexPQ`: codes via `pq.compute()`, codebooks via `pq.centroids`)\n— it does not accept dense vectors:\n\n```cpp\nfaiss::IndexRecJPQPrune index(d, M, B);       // METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT by default\nindex.build(n, item_codes, codebooks, ids);   // ids optional (default 0..n-1)\n```\n\n`item_codes` is a row-major `N x M` `uint8_t` matrix (code at split `m` of\nitem `i` at `item_codes[i*M + m]`); `codebooks` is row-major\n`M*B*d_split` floats (`G[m][b][j]` at `codebooks[(m*B + b)*d_split + j]`).\nAll data is copied (the index owns its storage). `build()` on a non-empty\nindex throws; use `reset()` first. `add()`/`add_with_ids()` throw\n(informative messages); `add_sa_codes()` appends RecJPQ codes (the CSR\nlists are rebuilt over the whole catalogue, so repeated calls are `O(N)`\neach); `sa_decode()` decodes codes back into approximate embeddings.\n\n## Inverted lists (CSR)\n\n`RecJPQInvertedLists` stores the `M*B` posting lists (list `(m, b)` =\npositions of the items whose code at split `m` is `b`) in CSR style:\n\n- `offsets`: `M*B + 1` boundaries;\n- `item_ids`: one contiguous array of `N*M` internal positions, in\n  ascending item order within each list.\n\nTwo-pass construction (count, prefix sum, fill), no per-list allocation, no\npadding for empty lists. Accessors: `list_size`, `get_list` (`nullptr` for\nempty lists), `get_list_range`, `total_entries`.\n\nThe posting storage is the dominant memory cost: `N*M*sizeof(idx_t)` bytes\n(e.g. 64 MB for `N = 10^6, M = 8`).\n\n## Scoring\n\nThe search uses the PQTopK scoring function: for query `phi`, the\n`M x B` sub-item score matrix is computed **once** per query\n\n```\nS[m][b] = dot(G[m][b], phi_m)\n```\n\n(M `sgemm` calls, `1 x d_split` by `d_split x B`), and each item is scored\nby a table lookup `score(i) = sum_m S[m][code(i,m)]` — no full dot product\nis computed during the search.\n\n## Search algorithm (Algorithm 1 of the paper)\n\nFor one query:\n\n1. Compute `S`, and sort the sub-item ids of each split by descending `S`\n   (ties: lower sub-item id first), keeping a per-split cursor.\n2. Upper bound: `sigma = sum_m S[m][next unprocessed sub-item of split m]`\n   (`-inf` for an exhausted split).\n3. Threshold: `theta` = score of the current `k`-th best item (`-inf` until\n   `k` items have been scored).\n4. While `sigma > theta`:\n   - pick the split `m*` whose next unprocessed sub-item scores highest\n     (ties: lowest `m` first);\n   - process the next `batch_size` sub-item ids of that split (clamped at\n     `B`);\n   - the union of their posting lists yields new candidate items\n     (deduplicated by internal position with a per-thread generation\n     counter);\n   - score the candidates with the `S` lookup table and merge them into the\n     running top-K (`partial_sort` of the union, keeping\n     `min(k, |union|)`);\n   - update `theta` and `sigma`.\n\n**Correctness / exactness.** Every item not yet scored has an unprocessed\ncode in every split, so its score is bounded by `sigma`; when `sigma <=\ntheta`, no unscored item can enter the top-K, and the result is the *exact*\ntop-K under the tie-breaking policy below. In exact mode (default) the loop\nruns until that condition holds — there is no iteration cap and no early\ntermination. If `max_iterations` (approximate mode only) is reached first,\nthe result is the best top-K over the items scored so far and\n`last_search_complete` is set to `false`.\n\n### Tie-breaking policy (deterministic)\n\nTies in item score are broken by **discovery order**: the item that first\nentered a candidate batch (earlier main-loop iteration, then earlier\nposition within the batch) ranks first. Implementation: each scored item\ncarries a per-query unique discovery sequence; the top-K merge orders by\n`(score desc, sequence asc)`. Sub-item id ties are broken by ascending sub\nitem id, and split ties by the lowest split index. With this policy an\nunscored item tying `theta` necessarily loses the tie-break against an\nalready scored one, so `sigma <= theta` remains an exact termination\ncondition (the paper's correctness argument, made deterministic).\n\n## Configuration\n\nIndex-level defaults (all written/read with the index):\n\n| member | default | meaning |\n|---|---|---|\n| `batch_size` | 8 | sub-item ids processed per main-loop iteration (`BS` in the paper) |\n| `max_iterations` | -1 | main-loop iteration cap; -1 = unlimited (ignored in exact mode) |\n| `ub_inflation` | 1.0 | threshold multiplier in approximate mode: stop at `sigma <= theta * ub_inflation` |\n| `exact_mode` | true | run to exact `sigma <= theta` termination (forces `ub_inflation = 1.0`, ignores `max_iterations`) |\n\n`SearchParametersRecJPQPrune` (passed to `search`) overrides these and can\npoint at a caller-owned `RecJPQPruneStats`:\n\n```\niterations, items_scored, postings_traversed, sub_items_processed,\nfinal_sigma, final_theta\n```\n\n(counters accumulate over the queries of one `search` call).\n\n`last_search_complete` (`std::atomic<bool>`) reports whether the most\nrecent `search` ran every query to exact termination.\n\n## Thread safety\n\n`search`, `reconstruct*`, `score_item`, `compute_sub_item_scores` and\n`sa_decode` are `const` and safe to call concurrently. Per-thread scratch\n(score matrix, sorted id lists, top-K, deduplication generation table) is\ncached in a bounded per-thread-state map; the deduplication table is a\n`uint32` generation counter per item, never shared between searches, and\nwraps safely (table cleared, generation restarted). `build`/`add_sa_codes`/\n`reset` take exclusive access and must not run concurrently with searches.\n\n## Persistence and cloning\n\n`write_index`/`read_index` support the index with fourcc `\"IRJQ\"` (layout:\nindex header, `M`, `B`, search defaults, item codes, ids, codebooks, CSR\noffsets and item ids; sizes are validated on read). `clone_index` produces\nan independent copy (the class is not copy-assignable because of its\ninternal mutexes). `reconstruct(key)`, `reconstruct_batch` and\n`reconstruct_n(i0, ni)` use external-id semantics (Faiss convention);\n`reconstruct_positions(i0, ni)` uses internal positions.\n\n## Differences from the paper / TF reference\n\n- **Termination.** The paper's Algorithm 1 iterates while `sigma > theta`\n  exactly as implemented. The TensorFlow reference (`pruned_score_batch.py`)\n  compares `sigmoid(sigma) > sigmoid(theta) * ub_inflation`; this is\n  algebraically identical at `ub_inflation = 1.0`. Here `ub_inflation` is\n  applied directly as `sigma <= theta * ub_inflation` (same effect, no\n  sigmoid).\n- **Batch scoring.** The TF reference scores only the top of each batch;\n  here all new candidates of a batch are scored. Both are exact; scoring\n  them all keeps the code simple and is the same asymptotic work, since\n  every candidate is scored at most once per query (deduplication).\n- **Storage.** The TF reference uses a dense, `-1`-padded inverted index;\n  the CSR layout here stores no padding.\n- **`B > 256` is not supported** (item codes are `uint8_t`); the paper does\n  not impose this limit.\n\n## Building and running\n\nThe index is registered in `faiss/CMakeLists.txt` (main library), the test\nin `tests/CMakeLists.txt`, and the benchmark/demo are `EXCLUDE_FROM_ALL`\ntargets:\n\n```\ncmake --build build --target faiss_test\n./build/tests/faiss_test --gtest_filter='*RecJPQ*'\n\ncmake --build build --target bench_recjpq_prune demo_recjpq_prune\nOMP_NUM_THREADS=1 OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 ./build/benchs/bench_recjpq_prune [N] [n_queries] [k] [random|structured]\n./build/demos/demo_recjpq_prune\n```\n\n## Benchmark results\n\nApple Silicon (M-series), clang 23, `-O3` Release, single OpenBLAS/OpenMP\nthread, `M = 8, B = 256, d_split = 64` (d = 512), `N = 10^6`, `k = 100`,\n100 unit-norm Gaussian queries. Codes uniform; `random` codebooks i.i.d.\nGaussian (hard case: no score hierarchy); `structured` codebooks = unit\ndirections scaled by log-normal magnitudes (emulates the wide spread of\nsub-item scores in real recommendation embeddings).\n\nMemory: build ~24 ms; index footprint **76.8 MiB** (8 MB codes + 8 MB ids +\n0.5 MB codebooks + 64 MB CSR postings).\n\nExhaustive PQTopK baseline (score all items + top-K selection):\n**3.6-3.7 ms/query**.\n\n| dataset | batch | median ms | p95 ms | items scored | % of catalogue | iterations |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| random | 1 | 7.06 | 8.02 | 537,807 | 53.8 | 187 |\n| random | 8 | 6.96 | 8.21 | 546,009 | 54.6 | 24 |\n| random | 64 | 11.30 | 11.94 | 809,006 | 80.9 | 5 |\n| structured | 1 | **1.40** | 2.30 | 116,867 | **11.7** | 32 |\n| structured | 2 | 1.41 | 2.34 | 121,624 | 12.2 | 16 |\n| structured | 8 | 1.86 | 2.67 | 166,047 | 16.6 | 5 |\n| structured | 64 | 10.10 | 11.24 | 671,771 | 67.2 | 4 |\n\nOn the structured catalogue the pruning scores ~12% of the items and is\n~2.6x faster than exhaustive; on purely random data there is no structure\nto exploit and the cost is comparable (this is a lower bound on the\noverhead of the machinery). Exactness: in both datasets the top-`k` score\nvectors match the exhaustive baseline bit-for-bit (max abs diff 0).\n\n`batch_size` trades work against parallelism within a batch: small batches\ndo the least total work (each sub-item's posting list is deduplicated\nagainst everything seen so far), while large batches traverse more postings\nbefore the threshold drops. `1..4` is the sweet spot in this configuration.\n\n## Limitations / future work\n\n- No GPU support; the inner loop is scalar (SIMD of the `S` lookups and the\n  merge are straightforward future work).\n- `add_sa_codes` rebuilds the CSR lists in `O(N)`; a true incremental CSR\n  append would need a re-merge of the posting arrays.\n- The per-query per-thread scratch is allocated on first use (a few hundred\n  KB at `B = 256`) and cached for the life of the thread pool.\n",

Summary

faiss::IndexRecJPQPrune (Petrov et al., SIGIR 2025) is implemented, tested, and benchmarked. All changes are uncommitted for your review.

Bugs fixed in this session

  • is_trained() shadowed the base Index::is_trained data member → removed
  • cblas.h not found → replaced with the repo's extern "C" sgemm_ convention (as in ProductQuantizer.cpp)
  • Zero-arg FAISS_THROW_IF_NOT_FMT in the IO read branch expanded to a trailing-comma snprintf → now passes the actual sizes in the messages
  • BLAS layout bugs (found by the tests, twice): ldc=1 illegal for a B×1 C matrix, then lda=d_split wrong for a 1×d_split row — final call is sgemm(1×B = (1×d_split)·(d_split×B)) with lda=ldc=1, ldb=d_split
  • ts.topk not cleared between queries on a reused thread state → stale entries/sequences leaked into the next query
  • get_list contract: now returns nullptr for empty lists as documented
  • Test bugs: sorted-vs-unsorted id comparison, rejecting legitimate negative ids, null-buffer reconstruct_positions loop (segfault), check_results taking std::string_view
  • API: build(0, nullptr, ...) allowed for empty catalogues

Test results

  • 22/22 new tests pass — inverted-list correctness, scoring vs full dot product, exact equivalence vs exhaustive PQTopK (6 configs × k ∈ {1, 7, 50, N/2, N, N+3} × batch sizes {1,2,4,8,16,64}), negative scores, all-equal scores, M=1/B=1, empty index, k>N, duplicate/non-contiguous/negative ids, reset+rebuild, add_sa_codes, reconstruct, validation throws, max-iterations incompleteness, 8-thread concurrency, IO round trip, clone, memory footprint
  • Full Faiss suite: 269 passed, 0 failed (5 pre-existing RISC-V skips)

Benchmark (N=10⁶, M=8, B=256, d=512, k=100, 100 queries, single-threaded BLAS)

  • Build ~24 ms; memory 76.8 MiB (64 MB of it CSR postings)
  • Exhaustive PQTopK baseline: 3.6–3.7 ms/query
  • Structured codebooks (log-normal magnitudes, emulating real recsys score hierarchy): 11.7% of catalogue scored at BS=1, median 1.40 ms → 2.6× faster than exhaustive
  • Random codebooks (no structure, worst case): 54% scored, ~7 ms — the honest lower bound on overhead
  • Exactness: top-k score vectors match exhaustive bit-for-bit (max diff 0) in both modes
